button_press.description: Press a button entity. A button is momentary and has no state to read back.

cover_close.description: Close a cover. ADVANCED, and the more dangerous direction: a closing cover is the one that can trap something.

cover_open.description: Open a cover. ADVANCED: a cover can be a garage door, a gate or a shutter — moving one has physical consequences a generic client cannot see.

cover_set_position.description: Drive a cover to a position. ADVANCED, as cover_open.

position.description: Target position on ESPHome's scale: 0.0 fully closed, 1.0 fully open. NOT a percentage — a 0-100 slider divides by 100 first. The node answers 409 if this cover does not report position at all.

cover_stop.description: Halt a cover mid-travel. Not every cover supports it.

entity_state.description: Read one entity's current state as JSON.

domain.description: Entity domain as the node reports it: sensor, binary_sensor, switch, light, cover, fan, climate, number, select, button, lock, text_sensor, valve, ...

entity.description: Entity identifier from the node's own state payload, percent-encoded. Name form on ESPHome >= 2026.1, slugified object_id before that.

entity_state_detailed.description: Read one entity's state with the extra descriptive fields, including a select's available options.

detail.description: Only `all` is defined; it adds name, device and (for a select) the option list.

entity_toggle.description: Flip an on/off entity. Do not send this without reading the state first — it is a flip, not a set.

entity_turn_on.description: Turn an on/off entity on — switch, light, fan.
entity_turn_on.notes: Optional query parameters depend on the domain: a light takes brightness (0-255), r/g/b (0-255), white_value, color_temp (mireds), effect, transition and flash (seconds); a fan takes speed_level and oscillation.

number_set.description: Set a number entity to a value within its own min/max, which the entity reports.

value.description: The new value. Outside the entity's range the node ignores it rather than clamping, so read the range from the entity first.

select_set.description: Set a select entity to one of its options.

option.description: One of the strings from the entity's option list (GET the entity with detail=all to obtain it). An unknown option is rejected.

methods.notes: The SRV port here is the native API's (6053), not the web server's — the service belongs to `api:`. A node without `api:` does not publish this service at all; see the _http._tcp method below. Use this method only after every product spec's txt_match has been tried: matching it first is what turns somebody's ESPHome thermometer into a garage-door opener.

txt_match.description: ESPHome's mdns component publishes version/mac/config_hash on the _http._tcp service only when the node has NO native API — otherwise those records live on _esphomelib._tcp. config_hash is the ESPHome-specific key of the three, so its presence is what separates this from the printers, routers and NAS boxes that also advertise _http._tcp.

methods.notes: For API-less builds, which publish no _esphomelib._tcp service at all. Weaker than that method in two ways. First, _http._tcp is every web server on the link, and this one leans entirely on the TXT set, so a node failing the config_hash condition is simply not matched here — not claimed by default. Second, the port is a convention, not a promise: ESPHome publishes this service for a build with NEITHER api nor web_server too (so that .local resolution works), and there nothing answers on 80. Treat a match as "an ESPHome node is at this address" and confirm with an actual request before offering anything.

discovery.notes: Key on the TXT `mac`, which survives a rename, a DHCP move and a reflash. Do not key on `config_hash` (it changes on every config change), on the friendly name (users rename and reuse), or on the address.

device.name: ESPHome Node (generic)
device.notes:
ESPHome is open-source firmware that turns an ESP32/ESP8266/RP2040/nRF52 (and LibreTiny-supported) board into a locally-controlled device. It is a PLATFORM, not a product: a node can be a temperature sensor, a plug, a bluetooth proxy, a presence sensor, a sprinkler valve, a garage-door controller, or a one-off somebody built on a breadboard. They all announce the same mDNS service type and all speak the same two APIs. What a node IS can only be learned by asking it — which is what this spec is for.
WHY THIS SPEC EXISTS. `_esphomelib._tcp.local.` is the service type of the firmware, so a consumer that maps a service type to a device spec labels every ESPHome node with whichever product spec claimed that service type first. That is not a hypothetical: with ratgdo.yaml the only claimant, every ESPHome node on the LAN rendered as a garage-door opener, complete with open/close controls that pointed at entities the node does not have. Product specs on this platform now carry an `identification.mdns_txt_match` on the project_name TXT record, and this spec is the deliberate catch-all (`platform_fallback: true`) for everything that matches none of them. That flag is set on the _esphomelib._tcp method ONLY: the _http._tcp method below is narrowed by a TXT condition and nothing else, because being the catch-all for a service type ESPHome does not own would rebuild this bug with printers in it.
WHAT identify_only MEANS HERE, AND WHAT WOULD CHANGE IT. `integration` says what a consumer of this registry actually DOES with a device, and today the honest answer for an unrecognised node is: name it, show it, and hand the user to its own web UI. Two facts hold that line. First, this file declares no `entities` and cannot — the control surface is whatever its owner compiled in — so a consumer has controls only once it implements the runtime enumeration described below, and until then there is nothing for it to draw. Second, the HTTP surface is OPTIONAL: `web_server:` is a choice the builder makes, and a great many nodes run `api:` alone and answer nothing on :80, so the `http_endpoints` and `commands` here describe a surface that may not exist on the node in front of you — they are the grammar for a client that has already found one, not a promise that every node has it. The native API is the surface that is always there, and it is documented here as prose because a length-delimited protobuf schema is not something this file can carry executably. When a consumer implements enumeration over either API, this spec becomes `supported` with no other change to it; that is the intended path, not a caveat about the platform's openness.
WHAT A NODE PUBLISHES ABOUT ITSELF (mDNS TXT on _esphomelib._tcp, from ESPHome's mdns component):
  friendly_name   the human name, absent when the config sets none
  version         the ESPHome version the firmware was built with
  mac             the board's MAC, the stable identity key
  board / platform  e.g. d1_mini / ESP32 — hardware, not function
  network         wifi | ethernet | thread
  config_hash     hash of the config, changes when the node is reflashed
  project_name / project_version   present only when the firmware sets
                  `esphome: project:` — this is what names a PRODUCT
                  ('ratgdo.v25iboard_secplus2'). A hand-rolled node has no
                  project_name at all, which is itself informative.
  api_encryption  the native API needs Noise with a PSK
  api_encryption_supported   the build can do Noise but has no key set, so
                  it still accepts plaintext
  api_provisioning=zero-psk  no key is set and one may be provisioned over
                  a zero-PSK Noise connection
  package_import_url   present on dashboard-importable builds
A node with NO native API publishes `_http._tcp` instead, carrying version/mac/config_hash. Two different builds land there: one with web_server (port 80 answers), and one with neither api nor web_server, which ESPHome still advertises so that .local resolution works at all — on that one nothing is listening on 80. So this service says "an ESPHome node lives at this address", not "there is an HTTP surface here": probe before offering one.
THE TWO LOCAL APIS. Both are direct device<->client; there is no cloud and no broker anywhere in ESPHome. 1. WEB SERVER (HTTP, port 80 by default) — present only when the config
   includes `web_server:`, which is a choice the builder made, so a node
   that answers nothing on :80 is normal rather than broken. Grammar:
     GET  /<domain>/<entity>            -> JSON state
     GET  /<domain>/<entity>?detail=all -> adds name/device and, for a
          select, its option list
     POST /<domain>/<entity>/<action>[?params]
     GET  /events                       -> text/event-stream
   Domains the web server routes (ESPHome 2026.8): sensor, binary_sensor,
   text_sensor, event, switch, button, fan, light, cover, number, date,
   time, datetime, text, select, climate, lock, valve,
   alarm_control_panel, update, water_heater, infrared, radio_frequency.
   Each is compiled in only when the node has one, so an unknown domain in
   an enumerated entity means a newer ESPHome, not a broken node — carry it
   through as read-only rather than dropping the entity.
   Sub-device entities insert a device segment: GET
   /<domain>/<device>/<entity>, POST /<domain>/<device>/<entity>/<action>.
2. NATIVE API (TCP 6053, protobuf) — what Home Assistant uses, and always
   present unless the builder removed `api:`. Length-delimited protobuf
   frames whose first byte is the indicator: 0x00 plaintext, 0x01
   Noise-encrypted (Noise_NNpsk0_25519_ChaChaPoly_SHA256, prologue ASCII
   "NoiseAPIInit", 32-byte base64 PSK from `api: encryption: key:`).
   Sequence: Hello -> Connect -> DeviceInfo -> ListEntities (each entity
   arrives with a numeric key) -> SubscribeStates; commands carry the key.
   The legacy `api: password:` was removed in ESPHome 2026.1.0. Richer and
   cheaper than HTTP, but much more work to implement — prefer the web
   server for a first client, and fall back to the native API for nodes
   built without one.

ENUMERATION — HOW A CLIENT LEARNS WHAT THIS NODE IS. There is no "list entities" URL on the web server. Connect to /events: on connect the node sends a `state` event for EVERY entity it has, so one connection yields the whole surface, and the same connection then carries live updates (plus `ping` keepalives and, when `log:` is on, `log` events). Each state event's JSON carries the entity identifier, its human `state` string and the typed value(s) for its domain. Build the UI from that list: the domain gives the control type, and the entity's own name is the label. On the native API the equivalent is ListEntities. Do not infer a device type from the product name, the board or the pictogram — the entity list IS the device.
ADDRESSING — WHICH IDENTIFIER GOES IN THE URL. ESPHome changed this, and a client that assumes one form silently breaks on the other half of the fleet:
  * ESPHome <= 2025.12: the URL segment is the entity's slugified object_id
    and the JSON `id` field is `<domain>-<object_id>` — /sensor/outside_temp,
    {"id":"sensor-outside_temp"}.
  * 2026.1.0 .. 2026.6: URLs match the entity NAME first and fall back to
    object_id with a deprecation warning, so both work. From 2026.1.3 the
    state JSON also carries `name_id` with the new-format identifier beside
    the legacy `id`.
  * 2026.7: the object_id fallback is gone from URL matching — URLs are the
    entity NAME, percent-encoded (/sensor/Outside%20Temp) — but the JSON
    `id` is STILL the legacy `<domain>-<object_id>`, with the new form in
    `name_id`. The two boundaries are one release apart, and this is the
    release that punishes a client for deriving a URL from `id`.
  * >= 2026.8: the JSON catches up. `id` itself carries
    `<domain>/<entity_name>` and `name_id` is no longer sent.
  The robust client reads the identifier out of the /events payload rather
  than deriving it: prefer `name_id`, else `id`, and treat an identifier
  containing '/' as the name form (split on the first '/' for the domain)
  and one containing '-' as the legacy form. Then send to the form the node
  handed you. A wrong identifier answers 404, never a silent no-op, so a
  client may also just try and fall back.

AUTH AND EXPOSURE. The web server has no auth unless the builder added `web_server: auth:`, and where the web-OTA platform is enabled anyone who can reach the node can flash it — which is upstream's own warning, not a defect of any one product. Cross-origin requests to entity endpoints are rejected unless the origin matches or is listed in `allowed_origins`, so a browser-based client needs the node's own address. None of this changes what a native app must do; it changes what it must not assume it may do from a web view.
SAFETY. Because a node can be anything, a generic client cannot know what a control does: `switch/Pump`, `cover/Gate` and `light/Desk` render identically. Treat cover, lock, valve, alarm_control_panel and climate actions as advanced — confirm before sending, show the reported state, and never fire one as part of a bulk action.

issued_to_client: The native-API Noise PSK, which the owner must hand to the client — a node with `api_encryption` in its TXT records will not talk protobuf without it
credentials.notes: Nothing here is issued by a vendor cloud; every secret is one the owner set when they built the firmware. A client should treat a missing PSK as "ask the owner", not as a failure to work around: the web server is the path that needs no secret, when the build has one.
stored_on_device: Native-API Noise PSK, when the build uses encryption

factory_reset.effect: ESPHome's factory reset invalidates every preference the node stored in flash and reboots: saved states, counters, globals, and — for a node configured through the captive portal — its Wi-Fi credentials, which takes the node off the network until it is provisioned again from its fallback AP. A native-API encryption key provisioned at runtime rather than set in YAML is likewise cleared. The FLASHED CONFIG is untouched, so the node comes back as its YAML describes it. Upstream's own warning applies: the data is physically erased and cannot be recovered. Whether a given node exposes the reset at all is the builder's choice — a hand-rolled node may expose none, and then re-flashing is the reset.

procedures.basis: ESPHome's documented factory_reset button and factory_reset switch components. Not run here, and present only when the node's config includes one — which is why this is the first thing to look for in the enumerated entity list rather than a step to assume.
procedures.description: A node whose config declares `button: - platform: factory_reset` (or the equivalent switch) exposes it like any other entity, so it appears in the /events enumeration and can be pressed over the web server or the native API. There is no confirmation step on the device — the press is the reset.
procedures.name: Factory Reset button or switch entity

steps.action: Enumerate the node's entities from GET /events and look for a button or switch whose name says factory reset.
Confirm with the owner that they mean to erase the node's stored preferences, including its Wi-Fi credentials if it was provisioned by captive portal.

steps.expect: The node reboots; preferences are cleared. A captive-portal-provisioned node does not come back on the LAN and must be re-provisioned from its fallback AP.

procedures.basis: The universal path for a node that exposes no reset entity: ESPHome firmware is installed over USB (esptool / the web installer) or by OTA, and a fresh install starts from the config's defaults.
procedures.description: Works on any node, needs physical access for the USB route, and is the only option when the config declares no factory_reset entity. Re-flashing replaces the config as well as clearing it, so it is also how a node changes what it is.
procedures.name: Re-flash the firmware

steps.action: Connect the board over USB (or reach it over OTA) and install the firmware image.
steps.expect: The node boots the newly flashed config and, unless credentials were flashed with it, raises its fallback AP for provisioning.

methods.description: Fallback hotspot + captive portal. When `wifi: ap:` and `captive_portal:` are configured, a node that fails to join its configured network for one minute raises its own AP using the credentials from the config; joining it opens (or you browse to) http://192.168.4.1/ where Wi-Fi credentials can be set and firmware uploaded. This is also the recovery path when a router is replaced.

steps.action: Join the node's fallback AP (SSID and password come from the node's own config, so they vary per build).
Open http://192.168.4.1/ and submit the new Wi-Fi credentials.
Find the node again on the LAN via _esphomelib._tcp (or _http._tcp for an API-less build) and read its TXT records.
steps.expect: TXT mac identifies the same board; project_name, when present, says which product it is.

methods.description: Improv over BLE (`esp32_improv:`), where supported by the build: the node advertises the Improv Wi-Fi service and takes credentials over GATT. ESPHome also ships Improv over serial for USB provisioning, which is the same protocol on a different link.

setup.notes: An ESPHome node is built and flashed by its owner, so "setup" here is the network half: how a flashed board joins Wi-Fi and becomes reachable. Confidence medium — these are ESPHome's documented flows, not ones this project has run. The device is on the LAN and answering before any of this spec's control surface applies.

rejoin.notes: Standard Wi-Fi rejoin, and the captive portal above is the in-place path when the old network is gone. Identity keys on the board MAC, so a DHCP move or a rename loses nothing.

testing.notes: Written from ESPHome's published documentation and its source, both authoritative — this is open firmware, not a reconstruction. No node has been driven from this file yet by this project. The two things worth confirming first on real hardware are which ADDRESSING generation a given board's firmware accepts (below) and that the entity list recovered from /events is enough to draw a UI without any per-product knowledge.

http_endpoints.description: text/event-stream. On connect the node emits one `state` event per entity, which is how a client enumerates a node it has never seen; the stream then carries updates as they happen, `ping` keepalives, and `log` events when logging is enabled. Each `state` payload identifies its entity (`name_id` where present, else `id`) and carries the same JSON the matching REST GET returns.
http_endpoints.name: Event Stream (enumeration + live state)

http_endpoints.description: Current state of one entity as JSON. Every domain returns `id` and a human-readable `state`; most add a typed `value` (a float for sensor, a bool for binary_sensor/switch/fan, 0.0..1.0 for cover position, the chosen string for select). `state` is a LABEL, not the full picture — a cover reads OPEN or CLOSED whatever it is doing, and its travel is in the separate `current_operation` (OPENING/CLOSING/IDLE). Fields a device cannot report are simply absent rather than null: a cover with no position support sends no `position` key, a light without colour no `color`. Add `?detail=all` for the entity's `name`, its sub-device `device` when it has one, and a select's `option` list.
http_endpoints.name: Entity State

http_endpoints.description: Same, for an entity that belongs to a sub-device of the node. Three- segment URLs are read as device+entity on GET and as entity+action on POST — the method is what disambiguates them.
http_endpoints.name: Sub-Device Entity State

http_endpoints.description: Perform an action on an entity. The action vocabulary is per domain: switch/light/fan turn_on|turn_off|toggle; cover open|close|stop|toggle|set; button press; number set; select set; lock lock|unlock|open; alarm_control_panel arm_away|arm_home|arm_night|arm_vacation|disarm. Parameters ride the query string. A 200 means the command was accepted, not that the device did it — read the state back.
http_endpoints.name: Entity Action

http_endpoints.description: The four-segment form, POST only: a GET against it is an error, because the fourth segment is always an action.
http_endpoints.name: Sub-Device Entity Action

covers: Enumerate every entity the node exposes and its current state
Drive any entity the firmware exposes as controllable
Subscribe to live state changes without polling
local_access.summary: Local by construction, and note that this says something different from `integration: identify_only` above: control is entirely possible here — the web server is served from the board and the native API is a direct socket, with no vendor account, no broker and nothing to shut down. What is missing is a consumer that enumerates a node's entities at runtime, not a way in.
